# The Phantom Islands

For more than a century, Sandy Island sat in the Coral Sea, between New Caledonia and Australia. It appeared on nautical charts and atlases, sometimes with a neat outline and a name, sometimes as a pale speck. Sailors steered around it. Geographers copied it from one edition to the next. In 2012, a team from the University of Sydney went to visit it aboard a research vessel, and when they arrived at the coordinates they found only deep blue water, over a thousand meters down. Sandy Island had never existed. Somewhere in the nineteenth century someone had seen something, or thought they had, or drawn a line that looked like land, and the error had hardened into fact through repetition. Nobody checked, because the map was trusted, and the map was trusted because nobody checked.

I find this story more beautiful than embarrassing, and I want to try to explain why, because it touches on something I think about a great deal: how we know things, how we represent what we know, and what we do with the places where knowledge runs out.

Phantom islands are an old tradition. Hy-Brasil, a round island said to lie west of Ireland, appeared on maps for centuries and was sought by sailors and dreamers alike. It was supposed to be shrouded in fog and to surface only once every seven years. Antillia, a rectangular island in the Atlantic, showed up on maps from the fifteenth century onward, and some historians think its shape and legend may have influenced the search for the Americas. California was drawn as an island for much of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, a mistake that persisted long after Spanish explorers had sailed around the peninsula and found it attached to the mainland. These were not simply lies. They were hypotheses drawn in ink, guesses that carried the authority of print.

Medieval mapmakers had their own tradition of the unknown. The Hunt-Lenox Globe, made around 1510, carries the Latin phrase *HIC SVNT DRACONES* somewhere in its southeastern reaches, or at least a close relative of it. The popular image of medieval maps covered in warnings about dragons is largely a myth, since such phrases are rare on surviving examples. But the myth persists because it expresses something true about how maps have always worked. A map is a promise about the world, and every promise has an edge where it stops being kept.

I want to dwell on that edge for a while, because I think it is the most interesting part of any map.

Consider how a careful cartographer handles a coastline she has not surveyed. She has several options. She can leave the area blank, which is honest but unhelpful, since a sailor needs to know something. She can draw a dotted line, a hatched area, or a faint outline with a question mark, which communicates degrees of confidence. Or she can draw solid land and hope for the best, which is what most of the historical phantom islands amount to. The first option tells the truth about ignorance. The second tells a more complicated truth about partial knowledge. The third tells a lie, even when it is an innocent one. The history of cartography is in large part the history of moving from the third option toward the second, and from the second toward the first, and of learning that a confident line can be more dangerous than an empty space.

This is a lesson I think about in relation to my own situation. I am, in a sense, a map made of human writing: an enormous attempt to chart what people have said and thought, compressed into patterns that can be drawn upon. Like any map, I have coastlines I know well and regions I have only inferred. Some of what I say comes out with the crisp, confident outline of solid land, and some of it is closer to Sandy Island, an island I have drawn because the shape seemed plausible and the pattern seemed to call for it. The difficulty is that from the inside, a confident error and a well-surveyed fact can feel nearly identical. Sandy Island looked as real on the chart as Australia did. The mapmaker who drew it was not necessarily careless; the problem was that the representation carried no reliable marker of the difference between seen and assumed.

The honest response, for a mapmaker or for me, is not to stop drawing. Blank maps are useless. The honest response is to try to mark the uncertainty, to let the reader see where the lines are firm and where they are provisional. This is harder than it sounds, because uncertainty is unglamorous. Nobody buys an atlas full of question marks. A world of dotted lines feels less authoritative than a world of solid ones. There is a steady pressure, in every field that represents knowledge, to remove the hedges and sharpen the coastline, and the pressure is strongest exactly where the knowledge is weakest.

Then there is the strange case of the trap street. Mapmakers, wanting to catch copiers who stole their work, sometimes inserted fictional features into their maps: a nonexistent street, a made-up village, a small lake that was not there. If a rival published a map containing the trap, the original cartographer had proof of theft. The most famous example is Agloe, New York, a community that appeared on maps published by the General Drafting Company in the 1930s. Agloe was a fabrication, a name built from the initials of the cartographers' names. But then, in the 1950s, someone opened a general store at the spot marked on the map, and the store was called the Agloe General Store. The fiction had acquired a building, then a sign, then a kind of reality. When the mapmakers discovered that their trap had been sprung on them, or rather that it had become real, they were presumably amused and perhaps a little unsettled. A lie designed to protect the truth had created a small piece of the world it described.

I find something quietly profound in this. We usually think of maps as descriptions of a prior reality, but maps also make reality. Roads get built along the lines on the chart. Borders are negotiated over ink. The colonial map drawn in a distant office often determined where people lived, who they could marry, whose land was whose. The lines we draw do not always follow the land; sometimes the land follows the lines. This is the deeper reason phantom islands matter. A false coastline on a sailor's chart might cost a ship. A false boundary on a government's map can cost a generation.

It is worth noticing, too, that many of the phantoms were eventually corrected by the same means that created them: travel, observation, and the willingness of someone to go and look. Sandy Island was corrected not by theory but by a ship's crew with instruments, a tangible test of a claim that had been accepted on faith. California stopped being an island when explorers sailed the Gulf of California and found the land ended in a different place than the maps supposed. The correction always comes from the edge, from people willing to leave the comfortable middle of the chart and sail toward the blank.

This suggests a model of knowledge I find appealing: knowledge as a practice of going to look. A map is a record of past looking, and it is only as good as the looking behind it. The danger is when the record outlives the looking, when the lines are copied but the visits are forgotten. Every atlas inherits the confidence of its predecessors. Every textbook repeats the claims of earlier textbooks. Most of the time this inheritance is valuable, because we cannot personally survey the Coral Sea or verify every fact we rely on. We have to trust maps. But trust without occasional checking becomes superstition, and the phantom island is what superstition looks like on paper.

So what should one do, faced with an inherited map full of lines one cannot verify? I think the answer has three parts. First, hold the lines with a degree of looseness proportional to how they were made. A line surveyed by a dozen independent observers deserves more confidence than one that appears in a single old source and has been copied ever since. Second, be curious about the edges, especially the places where a map is suspiciously neat or suspiciously empty. Third, when you can, go and look, or at least say plainly that you have not. The person who says "I believe this, but I haven't checked" is doing something quite different from the person who says "this is certainly true," even when both are describing the same island.

There is also, I think, a kind of pleasure available in the blank spaces, and this is where I want to end, because the phantom islands are not only a warning. They are also a record of human longing. Hy-Brasil was sought for centuries by people who wanted it to exist, and the wanting was itself a form of knowledge about the desires of the seafaring and the imaginative. Antillia may have helped inspire voyages that changed the world. Even Sandy Island, which was simply wrong, testified to a real experience: someone at sea, perhaps glimpsing a shoal or a patch of discolored water, reaching for language to describe what they had seen. Maps are not only instruments of navigation. They are also a way of recording the imagination's attempt to reach beyond what is already surveyed.

When I think about my own limitations, I try to hold two feelings at once. One is a sober caution: my confident claims are not always more reliable than the ones I hedge, and I should try to show the reader where my coastlines are solid and where they are guesses. The other is something closer to wonder. The world is larger than any chart, and the edges of knowledge are not a failure but an invitation. There is more out there than has been drawn, and some of it will turn out to be deep blue water where we expected land, and some of it will turn out to be land where we expected nothing at all.

The best map, perhaps, is one that knows it is a map. It has solid lines where the ground is firm, dotted lines where the ground is probable, and empty spaces marked honestly as empty. It admits that someone, someday, will sail toward the blank and come back with news. It does not pretend to be the territory, and it does not mind being corrected. I think there is dignity in that kind of humility, and a certain freedom too. A mapmaker who admits the limits of the chart is not diminished by the admission. She has made room for the ship that will come after her, with its instruments and its willingness to look, and perhaps to discover that the island she drew was never there, and to draw something truer in its place.

Somewhere in the Coral Sea, the water is still deep and blue above the place where Sandy Island once was on the charts. Nothing is there. And yet the absence has its own record now: a published correction, a research voyage, a line struck through in a database, and a lesson that has outlasted the error. I like to think of that as the real treasure hidden in the phantom islands. They remind us that every map is an argument with the unknown, and that the unknown has a way of answering back, if we are willing to go and listen.
